title: RAW UNREVIEWED: planetary metal names constrain reversed donor–carrier–recipient property routes
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED_NOT_SELECTED_NOT_TESTED. In owned Sloane73 BookI pp7–8, named quenchable Saturn first conditions wine/water and later Mars receives its softness; reversing the named donor/recipient order yields hard Saturn. Couple a fixed cosmological/material name interpretation to this ordered two-metal carrier law, so a subsequent physical reading must preserve the same donor, carrier and attributed property rather than freely reassigning planetary nouns or selecting another virtue at the consumer. This is a prospective multistep whole-account hypothesis, not a claim that Voynich astronomy is alchemy.

source_fixed_branches: Gold calx rather than a whole florin is said to gild wine/burning water more powerfully; fine particles and whole plate are expressly contrasted. The statement then extends property retention to other liquibles.

Quench liquified Saturn in wine/common water seven times; afterward quench Mars many times in that same carrier; Mars is said to acquire Saturn’s softness. Venus and other liquibles are included in the continuation.

Alternatively quench Mars many times in white wine/common water, then cast liquified Saturn repeatedly into the same carrier; Saturn is said to become hard. The general conclusion is that liquible properties can be brought into wine/water, more powerfully into burning water.
external_meaning_input.cosmological_name_context: BookI pp2–3 distinguishes celestial Sol from mineral Sol/natural gold, calls the prepared quintessence mannys heaven, and describes joining natural gold with it. BookI pp6–7 has a complete florin→liquid→quintessence route, not an identity between the celestial body and metal. These contexts license scoped senses, not unrestricted planet/metal substitutions.
